blocks.text: A reliability test shows that a gearbox shaft survives 2 million cycles. The report states 'the shaft performed well' and gives a graph with no axis labels. Six months later the designer cannot tell whether the test used the design load or half of it. A technical report is evidence that outlasts the people who wrote it, and a reader who cannot find the method, the numbers and their uncertainty cannot use it.

blocks.markdown: Technical writing has a single aim: a reader with the right background can understand **what was done, what was found and what it means**, and could check or repeat the work. Clarity comes from three habits. Give the document a **fixed structure** so the reader knows where to look; present **quantitative evidence** completely, with units and uncertainty; and **cite sources** so that facts can be traced and opinion is not mistaken for evidence.

rows: Title and abstract (or summary)
Let the reader decide in 30 seconds whether to read on
Purpose, method in one line, key results with numbers, main conclusion
Introduction
State the problem and why it matters
Background, objective or question, scope
Method
Allow the work to be repeated and judged
Equipment, specimens, procedure, conditions, analysis, assumptions
Results
Present what was found, without interpretation
Data in tables and figures, with units and uncertainty
Discussion
Interpret results and compare with theory or literature
Meaning, limitations, sources of error, comparison with specifications
Conclusions and recommendations
Answer the objective
Numbered findings supported by results; actions
References and appendices
Credit sources; hold raw data and derivations
Consistent citations; extra material
blocks.caption: Standard structure of a technical report (names vary by organisation).

blocks.title: Each section does one job
blocks.text: Results state facts; the discussion interprets them; the conclusions answer the original question using only what the results support. New data must not first appear in the conclusions.

blocks.title: Allocating content to the right section
blocks.prompt: A student tested five bonded aluminium lap joints in tension. Sort these items into report sections: (a) a statement that the joint failed at a mean load of 48.2 kN; (b) the adhesive type and cure schedule; (c) the observation that failure was cohesive in the adhesive layer, suggesting good surface preparation; (d) a table of the five failure loads; (e) the aim of finding the joint strength for a design with a 30 kN limit.

steps.text: Aim (e) is the objective: it belongs in the introduction.
Adhesive and cure schedule (b) are conditions needed to repeat the test: method.
The table of five failure loads (d) is data: results.
The cohesive failure mode and what it suggests (c) is interpretation: discussion; the mean failure load (a) is a result that is also summarised in the abstract and used in the conclusion.

blocks.answer: Introduction: e. Method: b. Results: d (and a). Discussion: c. Abstract and conclusions: a, with the comparison to 30 kN.

blocks.markdown: Numbers in a report must carry their **units** and an indication of their **uncertainty**. In a table, put the quantity and unit in the column heading (for example 'Failure load (kN)'), not in every cell. In a graph, label both axes with the quantity and unit, choose scales that show the data, plot individual points or means with **error bars** and say what they represent (for example 'bars show standard error, n = 5'). Caption every figure and table so that it can be understood alone, and refer to it in the text.

blocks.caption: Mean \bar{x}, sample standard deviation s and standard error u of the mean for n repeated measurements.

blocks.title: Reporting repeated measurements
blocks.prompt: The five lap-joint failure loads are 48.2, 47.9, 48.6, 48.1 and 48.4 kN. Calculate the mean, standard deviation and standard error, and write the result as it should appear in a report.

steps.text: Report with consistent decimal places: 48.2 +/- 0.1 kN (mean +/- standard error, n = 5). State what the plus-or-minus means.

blocks.answer: Mean 48.2 kN with a standard error of 0.12 kN (reported as 48.2 +/- 0.1 kN, n = 5).

rows: Graph with unlabelled axes and no units
Axes labelled 'Load (kN)' and 'Displacement (mm)'
Table with units repeated in each cell
Units in the column headings
Mean given as 48.2401 kN
Mean quoted to a precision consistent with its uncertainty
Error bars with no explanation
Caption states 'Error bars show standard error, n = 5'
blocks.caption: Presenting quantitative data.

blocks.markdown: Finally, **cite** everything that is not your own result or common knowledge. Choose one style and use it throughout: author-date (Harvard) such as '(Smith, 2020)' with an alphabetical reference list, or numeric (IEEE-style) such as '[3]' with the list in order of citation. A good reference allows the reader to find the source. Cite the original source where possible, and quote a standard by its designation and year.

blocks.title: Evidence versus opinion
blocks.text: **Evidence** is a claim that can be checked: a measurement with method and uncertainty, a calculation, or a cited source. **Opinion** is a judgement or preference not supported in this way. Both have a place in a discussion, but they must be distinguishable. Replace 'this design is clearly better' with 'this design had 12% lower peak stress (Table 3)'.

blocks.title: Plagiarism and unsupported claims
blocks.text: Using another person's text, figures or data without citing them is plagiarism, even if reworded. A manufacturer's brochure is a claim, not independent evidence, until it is supported by test data or a standard.

points: A technical report follows a fixed structure in which each section does one job: abstract, introduction, method, results, discussion, conclusions and references.
Quantitative data need labelled axes and column headings with units, a sensible number of digits, and an explicit statement of uncertainty (for example standard error and n).
Cite sources in one consistent style and keep evidence (checkable measurements and cited sources) distinct from opinion.

questions.stem: A busy manager has 30 seconds to decide whether a 40-page test report on a pump seal is relevant to a problem she is facing. Which part of the report should provide this?

options.text: The abstract or summary with key results and conclusions

questions.correctOptionText: The abstract or summary with key results and conclusions

distractorRationale.b: Correct: the abstract summarises the purpose, method, key results and conclusion.
distractorRationale.d: The method is detailed and would take longer to read.

questions.explanation: The abstract is designed for rapid decision making. It should state the purpose, key quantitative results and the main conclusion in a few sentences.

questions.stem: A colleague wants to repeat your fatigue test on a welded bracket. Which section must contain the specimen geometry, load ratio, frequency and failure criterion?

distractorRationale.a: The introduction states the problem and aim.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: the method describes the procedure and conditions in enough detail to repeat the work.
distractorRationale.d: The abstract summarises but does not carry full detail.

questions.explanation: Repeatability requires the full conditions and procedure, which belong in the method. A reader cannot judge or reproduce the results without them.

questions.stem: A student's conclusion says 'the new heat sink also performed well in the vibration test', but no vibration test appears in the method or results. What is wrong?

options.text: Nothing, since conclusions can introduce new findings
The conclusion contains a claim not supported by results presented earlier
The conclusion should have been in the abstract only

questions.correctOptionText: The conclusion contains a claim not supported by results presented earlier

distractorRationale.a: Conclusions must follow from the results.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: every conclusion must be traceable to the evidence in the results and discussion.
distractorRationale.d: The abstract should reflect the report, not replace the conclusions.

questions.explanation: Conclusions answer the report's objective using only the evidence presented. A claim with no supporting method or data cannot be verified by the reader.

questions.stem: Which presentation of results for a tensile test is best?

options.text: A graph with axes labelled 'x' and 'y' and no caption
A graph with axes labelled 'Stress (MPa)' and 'Strain (-)', plotted points, and a caption describing the specimen and test speed
A table with the unit written in every cell and no headings

questions.correctOptionText: A graph with axes labelled 'Stress (MPa)' and 'Strain (-)', plotted points, and a caption describing the specimen and test speed

distractorRationale.a: Axes must state the quantity and units.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: labelled axes with units and an informative caption make the figure understandable alone.
distractorRationale.c: Units belong in the column headings, and headings are needed.
distractorRationale.d: A figure without scales cannot be read quantitatively.

questions.explanation: A figure should be self-contained: quantities and units on both axes, a caption that explains the conditions, and a clear way to read values. Units in column headings of tables serve the same purpose.

questions.stem: Five repeated measurements of a shaft diameter are 12.1, 12.4, 12.3, 12.2 and 12.5 mm. Their sample standard deviation is 0.158 mm. Calculate the standard error of the mean in mm.
questions.explanation: The standard error is the standard deviation divided by the square root of the number of measurements: 0.158/sqrt(5) = 0.158/2.236 = 0.0707 mm. The mean is 12.30 mm, so the result could be reported as 12.30 +/- 0.07 mm (standard error, n = 5).

questions.stem: A force transducer reads 250 N with an expanded uncertainty of +/- 6 N. What is the percentage uncertainty of the reading?
questions.explanation: Percentage uncertainty equals the uncertainty divided by the reading times 100: 6/250 x 100 = 2.4%. Quoting it this way lets readers compare the quality of measurements of different sizes.

questions.stem: Which reference list is consistent in a report that uses the numeric (IEEE-style) system?

options.text: [1], [2], [3] in order of first citation in the text, each with full details
A mixture of author-date and numbers according to preference

questions.correctOptionText: [1], [2], [3] in order of first citation in the text, each with full details

distractorRationale.b: Correct: numbering in order of citation with complete details is consistent.
distractorRationale.d: Alphabetical order belongs to author-date systems, and the source types are not restricted.

questions.explanation: Whatever style is chosen, it must be applied consistently so readers can find each source. In a numeric system the sources are numbered in order of first citation.

questions.stem: The statement 'This bearing is clearly the best choice' is a piece of evidence as it stands.
questions.explanation: Without data or a cited source, the statement is an opinion. Evidence would give, for example, a measured life or cost comparison with units and uncertainty.

questions.stem: A student has tested a bolted flange joint for leakage at four tightening torques. Outline the structure of the report and say what belongs in each section, including what the abstract and conclusions should say.
markingGuide: Title and abstract: purpose, method, key results with numbers, main conclusion
Method: specimens, torque values, instruments, procedure, analysis
Results: table and graph of leakage versus torque with units and uncertainty
Discussion: interpretation, sources of error and comparison with specification
Conclusions and recommendations supported by results; references and appendices
questions.explanation: Marks are awarded for a logical structure with the correct material in each section. The abstract should contain numbers and the conclusions should answer the aim.

questions.stem: The following draft sentences appear in a report: (i) 'The new damper is obviously far better.' (ii) 'Manufacturer X says its seals last 20 000 hours.' (iii) 'Peak vibration fell from 4.8 to 3.1 mm/s RMS (Table 2).' Classify each as evidence or opinion, rewrite (i) and (ii) so that they are properly supported, and explain why consistent citation matters.
markingGuide: (ii) a claim from a source; not independent evidence until verified or cited
(iii) evidence: a measured value with reference to data
Rewrite (i) using data, for example the percentage reduction in vibration with reference to a table
Rewrite (ii) with a citation and a caveat that it is a manufacturer claim, or with test data
Consistent citation lets readers trace sources, check claims and credits original authors; avoids plagiarism
questions.explanation: The marker looks for a clear distinction between checkable evidence and unsupported judgement, plus rewrites that include data or a citation. Mention of traceability and academic integrity earns the final marks.
